Check: you see the four directories, the five empty files, fruits.txt and numbers.txt; wc -l prints 7 and 20000. → Navigation Redirects The root of the system: save the tree of /, only one level deep, into Reports/system.txt (look in man tree for the option that limits how deep tree goes); print Reports/system.txt with cat. Check: tree printed nothing on the display, and the file shows the main directories of the system: boot, dev, etc, home, proc, tmp, usr and var; bin is a link to usr/bin. → Output Append and overwrite: save the tree of /usr, one level deep, into Reports/tree.txt; append the tree of /var, one level deep, to Reports/tree.txt, and print the file; overwrite Reports/tree.txt with the tree of /home, one level deep, and print the file again. Check: after the append, the file has both trees: /usr with bin, lib and share, then /var with cache, lib and log; after the overwrite, it has only the tree of /home, with student. → Output Errors apart: with a single ls -a command, list /etc/skel (the files copied into the home directory of every new user) and /root (the home directory of the administrator), so that the list goes into Reports/list.txt and the error into Reports/errors.txt; print the two files. Check: nothing appears on the display when you run ls; Reports/list.txt has .bashrc and .bash_profile, and Reports/errors.txt has a Permission denied for /root. → Errors Append errors: run ls /root and save its error into Reports/errors.txt, overwriting the file; print /etc/shadow (the file with the passwords of the users) with cat, and append its error to Reports/errors.txt; print Reports/errors.txt. Check: Reports/errors.txt has two lines, one for /root and one for /etc/shadow: only root can read them. → Errors The users and the groups: copy /etc/passwd (the list of the users) into Reports/users.txt without cp: print it with cat and redirect the output into the new file; copy /etc/group (the list of the groups) into Reports/groups.txt in the same way; count the lines of the two copies and of the two originals with wc -l. Check: every copy has the same number of lines as its original. → Output Everything in one file: run ls -a /etc/skel /root so that both the list and the error go into Reports/all.txt, using &>, and print the file; run the same command again, this time with the older way, > Reports/all.txt 2>&1 (see the table of redirects), and print the file again. Check: both times, Reports/all.txt has the error for /root and the files of /etc/skel, and nothing appears on the display when you run ls. → Redirects Silence: search /etc and /usr for files called os-release with find, and throw the errors away so that you do not see any Permission denied message; print the content of /etc/os-release (the file that describes your distribution) with cat. Check: find prints only two paths, /etc/os-release and /usr/lib/os-release; /etc/os-release has the name and the version of your distribution, Fedora Linux. → Special Files Input from a file: sort /etc/shells (the list of the shells installed in the system) with sort, giving it the file with <; count the lines of /etc/passwd with wc -l, giving it the name of the file as a parameter; count them again, this time giving the file with <. Check: the shells in /bin come before the ones in /usr/bin; both counts are the same, but only the first wc prints the name of the file. → Input Type a file: run cat with a redirect, so that what you type goes into Reports/todo.txt; type three lines, then press Ctrl+D at the beginning of a new line to end the input; print the content of Reports/todo.txt. Check: cat Reports/todo.txt prints the three lines you typed. → Input Pipes: count the programs in /usr/bin with ls, wc -l and a pipe; count the entries in /etc (the configuration of the system) in the same way; show the long list of /etc (ls -l) one screen at a time, with less. Check: there are more than a thousand programs and a few hundred entries in /etc; less stops after every screen, and you quit it with q. → Pipes Search with grep: show the line of your user, student, from /etc/passwd (the list of the users); count the lines of /etc/passwd that contain nologin: these are the users of the services, which cannot log in; list the programs in /usr/bin whose name contains zip. Check: your line ends with /home/student:/bin/bash; most of the users have nologin; the list of programs has gzip and gunzip. → Searching for a Text Repeated lines: run uniq fruits.txt and find out why it does not remove anything; print every fruit from fruits.txt only once; print every fruit with the number of times it appears, the most frequent first; print only the fruits that appear exactly once (look in man uniq). Check: uniq fruits.txt prints the same 7 lines, because no line is the same as the one above it; after sort, you get 4 fruits, 3 apple is the first line of the count, and only cherry and kiwi appear exactly once. → Repeated Lines Zeros and random bytes: show the first 16 bytes of /dev/zero in hexadecimal, with head and xxd; show the first 16 bytes of /dev/urandom in the same way, and run the command twice. Check: the bytes of /dev/zero are all zeros; the bytes of /dev/urandom are different every time you run the command. → Special Files Processes My shell: print the PID of your shell; list the processes of the terminal with all the columns of -f; show only the Name, State, Pid and PPid lines of the /proc/<PID>/status file of your shell, using grep (put the PID of your shell instead of <PID>). Check: ps and status show the same PID and PPID for bash, and its state is S. → Listing Processes · The /proc File System Inspect a process: in the second terminal, run sleep 1000; in the first terminal, find the PID of sleep with pgrep; print its /proc/<PID>/status file; print its command line, from /proc/<PID>/cmdline, with cat -v; find out its program and its current directory, from the links /proc/<PID>/exe and /proc/<PID>/cwd; stop sleep with Ctrl+C in the second terminal. Check: the state is S, the command line is sleep^@1000^@, the program is /usr/bin/sleep, and the current directory is the one of the second terminal. → The /proc File System Open files: list the File Descriptor Table of your shell, from /proc/$$/fd; in the second terminal, run sleep 1000; in the first terminal, find the PID of sleep and list its File Descriptor Table; stop sleep with Ctrl+C and try to list its table again. Check: 0, 1 and 2 point to a /dev/pts/... file, a different one for each terminal; after Ctrl+C, /proc/<PID> no longer exists. → The /proc File System The system: Find out about your computer using only the files in /proc: the model of the processor: the model name lines of /proc/cpuinfo (use grep); how many processors you have: count the processor lines of /proc/cpuinfo; the total memory: the MemTotal line of /proc/meminfo; for how many seconds the system has been running: the first number in /proc/uptime; the version of the kernel: /proc/version. Check: the number of processors is the same as the one printed by nproc, the time matches the up part of uptime, and the version of the kernel is the same as uname -r. → The /proc File System top and htop: start top, sort the processes by memory, then by processor, and quit; start htop, find your bash with a search, show the processes as a tree, and quit. Check: top shows the Tasks line with the number of processes in every state; in the tree of htop, your bash is under the terminal. → top · htop Archives and compression Three compressors: delete numbers.txt.gz, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with gzip, with bzip2 and with xz, keeping the original file every time; compare the sizes of the four files with ls -l. Check: you have numbers.txt, numbers.txt.gz, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, and the .xz file is the smallest. → Compressing One File How much smaller: delete numbers.txt.gz, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with gzip, with bzip2 and with xz, keeping the original file, so that each of them prints how much smaller the file got (look in their manual pages for the option that prints more details). Check: gzip and bzip2 printed how much they saved, as a percentage, and the one of bzip2 is larger; xz printed a ratio instead (about 0.045, the new size divided by the old one), so it saved about 95%, the most of the three. → Compressing One File Decompress: delete numbers.txt.gz and numbers.txt.bz2, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with gzip, without keeping the original, and check with ls that numbers.txt is gone; get numbers.txt back from numbers.txt.gz; compress numbers.txt with bzip2, keeping the original, then delete numbers.txt; get numbers.txt back from numbers.txt.bz2, this time keeping the compressed file. Check: wc -l numbers.txt prints 20000 both times; numbers.txt.gz is gone (gunzip deleted it, like gzip deletes the original), but numbers.txt.bz2 still exists. → Compressing One File What kind of file: delete numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, if they exist; compress numbers.txt with bzip2 and with xz, keeping the original; find out the types of numbers.txt, numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz, with a single file command; delete numbers.txt.bz2 and numbers.txt.xz; find out the type of /usr/share/man/man1/ls.1.gz, the manual page of ls. Check: file says ASCII text, bzip2 compressed data and XZ compressed data, and gzip compressed data for ls.1.gz: the manual pages are stored compressed with gzip, and man decompresses them when you read them. → Which One to Use A tar archive: create Archives/music.tar with the directories Music and Photos and the file fruits.txt; list the content of the archive; find out the type of the archive with file. Check: the archive has Music/, Photos/, the five empty files and fruits.txt, and file says POSIX tar archive. → Archives Extract: create Archives/music.tar with Music, Photos and fruits.txt (if it already exists, tar overwrites it); create the directory /tmp/extract; extract Archives/music.tar into /tmp/extract. Check: tree /tmp/extract shows Music, Photos and fruits.txt, with the same files as in ~/lab03. → Archives Only one file: create Archives/music.tar with Music, Photos and fruits.txt; create the directory /tmp/single; extract only Photos/dog.jpg from Archives/music.tar into /tmp/single. Check: tree /tmp/single shows Photos/dog.jpg, and nothing else. → Archives Add a file: create Archives/music.tar with Music, Photos and fruits.txt; add numbers.txt to Archives/music.tar, without creating the archive again; list the archive with the details of every file. Check: numbers.txt is the last file in the list, with the size 108894. → Archives Compressed archives: create Archives/all.tar with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; create Archives/all.tar.gz, Archives/all.tar.bz2 and Archives/all.tar.xz, each with the same three entries, compressed with gzip, bzip2 and xz; compare the sizes of the four archives with ls -l. Check: the .tar is the largest and the .tar.xz the smallest. → Compressed Archives List compressed archives: create Archives/all.tar.gz, Archives/all.tar.bz2 and Archives/all.tar.xz, each with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; list the content of each archive, without telling tar how it is compressed; find out the types of the three archives with file. Check: all three lists are the same; file shows a different compression for each of them. → Compressed Archives Extract compressed archives: create Archives/all.tar.gz, Archives/all.tar.bz2 and Archives/all.tar.xz, each with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; create the directories /tmp/gz, /tmp/bz2 and /tmp/xz; extract each archive into its own directory: the .tar.gz into /tmp/gz, the .tar.bz2 into /tmp/bz2 and the .tar.xz into /tmp/xz; show the three directories with tree. Check: the trees of the three directories are the same. → Compressed Archives A zip archive: delete Archives/all.zip, if it exists (zip would update it, not create it again); create Archives/all.zip with Music, Photos and numbers.txt, with everything inside the directories; list the content of the archive; extract it into /tmp/unzipped. Check: unzip -l lists 8 entries, and tree /tmp/unzipped shows Music with three files, Photos with two files, and numbers.txt. → Zip Archives Update a zip archive: delete Archives/all.zip, if it exists; create Archives/all.zip with Music, Photos and numbers.txt, with everything inside the directories; add fruits.txt to Archives/all.zip; list the files in the archive with zip -sf; extract only fruits.txt from the archive into /tmp/fruit. Check: zip -sf Archives/all.zip lists fruits.txt as the last file, and /tmp/fruit has only fruits.txt. → Zip Archives

Order matters: run ls /etc/skel /root > Reports/a.txt 2>&1 and print Reports/a.txt; run ls /etc/skel /root 2>&1 > Reports/b.txt and print Reports/b.txt; find out why the error is in a.txt, but not in b.txt. Check: the second command printed the error on the display. The shell reads the redirects from left to right, and 2>&1 makes 2 go where 1 goes at that moment. → Redirects See and save: In a single command line, save the list of the programs in /usr/bin into Reports/programs.txt and count them (look in man tee for the command that writes its input both to a file and to its output). Check: the number printed is the same as wc -l < Reports/programs.txt. → Pipes Redirects seen from inside: in the second terminal, run sleep 900 < ~/lab03/fruits.txt > /tmp/out.txt 2> /dev/null; in the first terminal, find the PID of sleep and list its File Descriptor Table; stop sleep with Ctrl+C in the second terminal. Check: 0 points to fruits.txt, 1 to /tmp/out.txt and 2 to /dev/null: the shell changed the table before sleep started. → The /proc File System · Redirects A pipe seen from inside: in the second terminal, run sleep 800 | sleep 900; in the first terminal, find the PIDs of the two sleep processes (look in man pgrep for the option that also prints the command line, so you can tell them apart); list the File Descriptor Tables of both processes; stop them with Ctrl+C in the second terminal. Check: 1 of sleep 800 and 0 of sleep 900 point to the same pipe:[...], with the same number. → The /proc File System · Pipes What does less read: in the second terminal, open /etc/services (the list of the network services and their ports) with less; in the first terminal, find the PID of less; list the files that less has open, and print its command line and its current directory, using /proc; quit less with q. Check: besides 0, 1 and 2, less has /etc/services open, at file descriptor 3 or higher. → The /proc File System Where is the other shell: in the second terminal, go to ~/lab03/Music and print the PID of the shell; in the first terminal, find the current directory of that shell, using /proc; open its environ file with less and find the value of the HOME variable (the \0 bytes between the variables show up as ^@; search with /). Check: cwd points to /home/student/lab03/Music, and environ has HOME=/home/student. → The /proc File System Save top: run top so that it prints its list only once and does not update it (see the tip in top); keep only the first 15 lines of its output, and save them into Reports/top.txt, in the same command line. Check: Reports/top.txt has 15 lines, starting with the summary of top. → top · Pipes htop in depth: In htop: hide the threads; show only your processes; sort them by memory; choose your bash and show its open files; add the PPID column, from the setup menu (F2). Check: the open files of bash are the same as in ls -l /proc/$$/fd, and the PPID of bash is the PID of the terminal. → htop Whose processes: count the processes of root with ps, wc -l and a pipe (look in man ps for the option that selects the processes of a user, and use --no-headers, so that wc -l does not also count the line with the names of the columns); count your own processes in the same way; count them again, without --no-headers. Check: root has many more processes than student: most of the system runs as root. Without --no-headers, each number is larger by one. → Listing Processes · Pipes Who runs the processes: list all the processes of the system with ps, printing only the column of the user, without the header line; in the same command line, using sort and uniq, print every user only once, with the number of its processes in front of it, the user with the most processes first. Check: the first line is root, with the same number as ps -u root --no-headers | wc -l, and student is among the first lines; the numbers added up are the same as ps -e --no-headers | wc -l. → Listing Processes · Repeated Lines Big files: create Archives/zeros.bin with the first 10 MB of /dev/zero, using head (look in man head for the option that prints a number of bytes instead of lines); create Archives/random.bin with the first 10 MB of /dev/urandom, in the same way; compress both files with xz, keeping the originals; compare the sizes of the four files with ls -lh; delete the four files: they are big. Check: zeros.bin.xz is a few KB, random.bin.xz is still about 10 MB: random data cannot be compressed. → Special Files · Compressing One File Compress into another file: Compress /etc/services (the list of the network services) without copying it and without changing /etc: use the option -c, which writes the compressed data to the standard output, and a redirect. compress it with gzip into Archives/services.gz; compress it with bzip2 into Archives/services.bz2; compress it with xz into Archives/services.xz; put time in front of each of the three commands, and compare the times and the sizes of the files. Check: the three files exist, /etc/services is unchanged, xz makes the smallest file and takes the longest. → Compressing One File Read without extracting: Look in man gzip and man xz for the commands that print the content of a compressed file, without creating any new file. compress /etc/services with gzip -c into Archives/services.gz, and with xz -c into Archives/services.xz; print the content of Archives/services.gz; count the lines of Archives/services.xz; print the first 20 lines of the compressed manual page /usr/share/man/man1/ls.1.gz. Check: the count is the same as wc -l < /etc/services; the manual page is a text file with formatting commands, lines that start with ., like .TH and .SH. → Compressing One File Compression from the name: create Archives/photos.tar.bz2 with Photos, without telling tar the compressor: let it choose the compressor from the extension of the archive (look in man tar for this option); find out the type of the archive with file. Check: file Archives/photos.tar.bz2 says bzip2 compressed data. → Compressed Archives Without the full path: create /tmp/doc.tar.gz with the directory /usr/share/doc/bash (the documentation of bash), so that the names in the archive start with bash/ and not with usr/share/doc/ (look in man tar for the option that changes the directory before adding the files); list the content of the archive. Check: tar tf /tmp/doc.tar.gz lists names that start with bash/. → Archives

Count with /proc: count the directories in /proc whose name is a number; count the processes of the system with ps -e --no-headers and wc -l; compare the two numbers. Check: the two numbers are almost the same: every process is a directory in /proc. → The /proc File System The shells of the users: Every line of /etc/passwd has 7 fields separated by :, and the last one is the shell of the user. print only the shell of every user (look in man cut for the options that choose the separator and keep only one field of every line); in the same command line, print every shell only once, with the number of users that have it, the most used first; print only the shells that are used by more than one user. Check: /usr/sbin/nologin is the first line, with most of the users; /sbin/nologin is the same program (/sbin is a link to usr/sbin), but uniq compares only the text, so it counts it on its own line; /bin/bash is used by root and student; the numbers added up are the same as wc -l < /etc/passwd. → Repeated Lines · Pipes Who has the file open: in the second terminal, open /etc/hosts (the names of the computers that the system knows without asking the network) with less; in the first terminal, find the file descriptor that points to /etc/hosts, without using pgrep or ps: search /proc/*/fd with find (look in man find for the test that checks where a symbolic link points to), and throw away the Permission denied errors for the processes of other users; check with ps -p that the number in the path that find prints is the PID of less; quit less with q. Check: find prints a path like /proc/3402/fd/4, and ps -p 3402 shows less. → The /proc File System Back up the configuration: create /tmp/etc.tar.gz with the whole /etc directory (the configuration of the system), except /etc/pki, the directory with the certificates that the system uses to check secure connections, like the https:// websites (look in man tar for the option that leaves files out of the archive); in the same command, save the errors of tar into Reports/etc-errors.txt; count the files in the archive, using the list that tar prints and wc -l; count the errors in Reports/etc-errors.txt. Check: tar tf /tmp/etc.tar.gz lists etc/passwd and etc/os-release, but nothing from etc/pki; Reports/etc-errors.txt has a Permission denied for every file that only root can read, like /etc/shadow. Its first line is tar: Removing leading `/' from member names: this is not an error, tar only tells you that it saves /etc/passwd as etc/passwd, so that the archive can be extracted anywhere, not only over /etc. Do not count it with the errors. → Compressed Archives Strip a directory: create Archives/all.tar.gz with Music, Photos and numbers.txt; create the directory /tmp/flat; extract Archives/all.tar.gz into /tmp/flat so that the files of Music and Photos end up directly in /tmp/flat, without their directories (look in man tar for the option that removes directories from the beginning of the names). Check: tree /tmp/flat shows the five empty files directly under /tmp/flat, but not numbers.txt. --strip-components=1 removes the first part of every name: Music/jazz.mp3 becomes jazz.mp3, but numbers.txt is in the top directory of the archive, so nothing is left of its name, and tar does not extract it (the same happens to the names Music/ and Photos/). → Archives Archives through a pipe: create /tmp/music.tar.gz with the directory Music, in a single command line, so that tar writes the archive, not compressed, to its standard output (an archive file named - means the standard output), gzip compresses it in a pipe, and a redirect saves it; create the directory /tmp/piped; extract /tmp/music.tar.gz into /tmp/piped in another pipe: gunzip -c decompresses it to its standard output, and tar reads the archive from its standard input (an archive file named - means the standard input). Check: file /tmp/music.tar.gz says gzip compressed data, and tree /tmp/piped shows Music. → Pipes · Compressed Archives Clean up: With a single rm command, delete everything that the exercises create in /tmp, without any error for the ones you did not create (look in man rm): the directories /tmp/extract, /tmp/single, /tmp/gz, /tmp/bz2, /tmp/xz, /tmp/unzipped, /tmp/fruit, /tmp/flat and /tmp/piped; the files /tmp/out.txt, /tmp/doc.tar.gz, /tmp/etc.tar.gz and /tmp/music.tar.gz. Check: rm prints nothing, and ls /tmp no longer shows them. → Managing Files

Use the last 5 minutes of the lab to answer these questions together with your colleagues and the teaching assistant. There are no wrong answers for the last two. What are the file descriptors 0, 1 and 2, and where do they point to in a terminal? What is the difference between > and >>? And between > and 2>? Why does wc -l < file not print the name of the file? What is the difference between an archive and a compressed file? Why does a .tar.gz have two extensions? When would you use .tar.xz, and when .zip? What is the difference between a program and a process? What are the PID and the PPID? Where are the files in /proc stored? What can you find out about a process from /proc that ps does not show? When would you use top, and when htop or btop? Which redirect or archive format will you use most often?
